item.title: Former national rugby player Paula Kata jailed for raping woman in her Canberra home
item.description: A former Tongan national rugby player has been sentenced to two and a half years in prison for raping a woman inside her own home in the Australian capital, Canberra. Paula Fala Kata, 38, was sentenced in the ACT Supreme Court on Wednesday, November 25, after a jury found him guilty of sexual intercourse without consent and committing an act of indecency without consent.
item.content:encoded:
A former Tongan national rugby player has been sentenced to two and a half years in prison for raping a woman inside her own home in the Australian capital, Canberra.

Paula Fala Kata, 38, was sentenced in the ACT Supreme Court on Wednesday, November 25, after a jury found him guilty of sexual intercourse without consent and committing an act of indecency without consent.

Justice Belinda Baker set a non-parole period of 15 months, making Kata eligible for release on parole in February 2028.

Region Canberra reported that Kata went uninvited to the woman’s home on the morning of Sunday, June 30, 2024, after she had blocked his messages.

The court heard that he kissed the woman without her consent before digitally raping her, despite her saying no and attempting to push him away.

The woman reported the assault to police that day, and a subsequent hospital examination identified physical injuries.

Kata was arrested and refused bail when he appeared before the ACT Magistrates Court the following day.

During sentencing, Justice Baker acknowledged the ongoing emotional impact of the assault on the victim and rejected Kata’s suggestion that she might have fabricated her account to obtain victims’ compensation.

Kata played professional rugby between 2007 and 2018, representing Tonga internationally before an injury ended his sporting career. He subsequently worked in Canberra’s construction industry.

Before his latest convictions, Kata had no criminal convictions.

In September 2023, he was acquitted by an ACT Supreme Court jury of two unrelated sexual offence charges stemming from an alleged incident at the Lyneham Motor Inn in April 2022.

item.title: Striking coach ‘Apikotoa remains key figure in former UFC champion Adesanya’s bid to revive career
item.description: Tongan striking coach Tristam ‘Twist’ Apikotoa has retained his place in former two-time UFC middleweight champion Israel Adesanya’s coaching team following a major restructuring of the internationally renowned fighter’s training programme. item.content:encoded:
Tongan striking coach Tristam ‘Twist’ Apikotoa has retained his place in former two-time UFC middleweight champion Israel Adesanya’s coaching team following a major restructuring of the internationally renowned fighter’s training programme.

Apikotoa is helping Adesanya prepare for his 5 December fight against Russian middleweight contender Shara ‘Bullet’ Magomedov in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, following four consecutive defeats and his departure from longtime Auckland gym City Kickboxing.

Now based at Unity MMA in Rosedale, Auckland, Apikotoa is working alongside Adesanya’s former wrestling coach Andrei Paulet, who has taken over as head coach.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Freestylebender, Adesanya explained that Paulet had brought Apikotoa into the new coaching arrangement because of his longstanding involvement in his training.

Apikotoa has also recruited sparring partners from South Auckland to strengthen preparations for the upcoming contest.

Adesanya told the New Zealand Herald that the revamped training programme had renewed his enthusiasm for fighting, saying he believed he could continue competing until the age of 45.

“The way this is the standard now, I can do this for as long as I want to,” Adesanya said.

Apikotoa’s technical knowledge and coaching abilities have previously earned praise from internationally successful fighters.

In an earlier interview with Pacific media platform The Coconet TV, Adesanya described him as underrated, while fellow UFC fighter Dan Hooker called him his “secret weapon”.

Born in New Zealand but raised in Tonga until the age of eight, Apikotoa is the son of Alisi Peau Ave-ika-Ki-Moana Wolfgramm from Neiafu, Vavaʻu, and Sosefo Losino Apikotoa Sapaʻata, whose roots lie in Niuafoʻou and Hihifo, Niuatoputapu.

Both families eventually settled in Fasi-moe-Afi, Tongatapu.

Apikotoa returned to New Zealand with his family in 1983, growing up in Onehunga and Māngere before attending St Peter’s College in Auckland.

His competitive kickboxing career in 1996 at Balmoral Lee Gar under renowned Tongan martial arts coach Lolo Heimuli.

Weighing 168kg when he first approached Heimuli about becoming a fighter, Apikotoa reduced his weight to 130kg within approximately six months to earn his first novice fight. He subsequently brought his weight down to 118kg.

His energetic fighting style earned him the nickname ‘Twister’, while his passion for studying and analysing fights later became a foundation of his coaching career.

Among his greatest inspirations was his uncle, Alex Tuʻitavake, better known as Alex Tui, whom Apikotoa described as Australia’s first world kickboxing champion. He regularly travelled to Australia during his holidays to train under him.

item.title: Tonga ranks second globally for adult obesity despite years of health strategies, as NCDs account for 85% of deaths
item.description: More than a decade of national health strategies has yet to reverse Tonga’s rising obesity rates, with the Kingdom now ranking among the world’s worst-affected countries for both adult and childhood obesity, while non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for approximately 85 percent of all deaths. item.content:encoded:
More than a decade of national health strategies has yet to reverse Tonga’s rising obesity rates, with the Kingdom now ranking among the world’s worst-affected countries for both adult and childhood obesity, while non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for approximately 85 percent of all deaths.

The latest World Health Organization (WHO) figures place Tonga second globally for adult obesity, with prevalence climbing from 54.4 percent in 2000 to 73.8 percent in 2024, while the Kingdom ranks third for obesity among children and adolescents.

The statistics were presented by WHO Pacific team coordinator Dr Tomo Kanda at Tonga’s National NCD Forum, held from 11–13 November in Nukuʻalofa.

Obesity prevalence among children and adolescents aged five to 19 has reached 32.6 percent, while 56.4 percent are classified as overweight, including those with obesity, placing Tonga fourth globally for childhood and adolescent overweight.

The historical figures raise questions about the effectiveness of successive government policies and interventions designed to address one of the Kingdom’s most pressing public health challenges.

In 2010, Tonga introduced its National Strategy to Prevent and Control Non-Communicable Diseases 2010–2015, followed by the Hala Fononga National Strategy 2015–2020 and a subsequent strategy covering 2021–2030.

These initiatives have sought to promote healthier diets, encourage physical activity and reduce risk factors associated with diabetes, cardiovascular disease and other chronic illnesses.

Government interventions have also included taxation targeting unhealthy food consumption, public awareness campaigns and community-based health promotion programmes.

However, adult obesity prevalence increased from 61.4 percent in 2010 to 70.2 percent in 2020, representing an overall increase of 12.4 percentage points between the introduction of the 2010 strategy and 2024.

Tonga continues to face significant challenges associated with dietary habits, dependence on imported foods, limited physical activity and the affordability of healthier food alternatives.

The Ministry of Health recently indicated that it was developing a plan to examine the economic impact of NCDs, according to the Tonga Broadcasting Commission.

The economic consequences potentially include increased healthcare expenditure, reduced workforce productivity and financial hardship for families caring for relatives with chronic illnesses.

While the rising obesity figures alone do not establish that individual government interventions have failed, they warrant closer examination of how national health strategies have been funded, implemented and evaluated.

The challenge facing health authorities is to demonstrate what measurable progress has been achieved through successive national strategies and identify what policy changes are needed to reverse a trend that has persisted for more than two decades.
